keyVerseText: Let the husband render unto the wife due benevolence: and likewise also the wife unto the husband.
rootMeaning: The root of εὔνοια (eúnoia) lies in the verb εὐνοέω (eunoéō), which means to be well-minded or reconciled. This etymology highlights an inward disposition of goodwill or kindness that is not merely external favor but a heartfelt alignment of mind and intention toward another. Thus, beyond the common English gloss of 'benevolence' or 'good will,' the root sense emphasizes a reconciled, positive mindset that fosters harmonious relationships.
usageInScripture: εὔνοια appears only twice in Scripture, consistently translated as 'benevolence' or 'good will.' This limited but focused usage underscores the word's association with acts of kindness and favor grounded in genuine goodwill. The consistency in translation reveals a clear semantic range centered on positive, voluntary kindness that may also euphemistically relate to marital duties, reflecting relational harmony and care.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding εὔνοια in its original sense enriches our grasp of Christian love as not merely external action but as a disposition rooted in reconciliation and heartfelt goodwill. This aligns with the biblical call to live in unity and mutual care, reflecting the character of God who is gracious and benevolent toward His people. The word's use in contexts such as marriage highlights the sacredness of relational kindness as a duty and delight, mirroring Christ's self-giving love for the church.
keyVerseReflection: In 1 Corinthians 7:3, Paul instructs husbands and wives to render to each other 'due benevolence,' using εὔνοια to emphasize the necessity of sincere goodwill and kindness in marital relations. This term conveys more than obligation; it implies a willing, reconciled heart that honors the spouse, reflecting the mutual care and respect foundational to Christian marriage. Thus, εὔνοια enriches the verse by underscoring the quality of love that should characterize the conjugal relationship.
